entries.text:
You don't perform. You set the psalter down, give the plain truth in order, and keep your hands still. Your Persuasion check was a 22, and the hall hears it.

You tell them about nineteen years of tales told for coin, the ledger, the three houses, and the two weeks you kept it because you didn't know whom to trust. You say it was partly curiosity, and you don't dress that up. When you name Edric Verrel's confession and Lady Maren's village, a few of the Vantry household look at their boots. Kit, at the wall, gives one slow nod.

The arbiter lets you finish. Then she lays her stylus flat. "A thief who confesses the theft before the thing stolen is the only one I have met who didn't need a cellar to be honest." The corner of her mouth moves slightly. "The leaf is admitted. The sealing is stayed. A rider goes to the keep's justice tonight, and another to Dame Crowe at Marrowford. You will swear to the ledger before the justice, and you will not leave Saltmarsh until he has heard you. I think that is a small price."

Sir Corwen stands, stiffly. "The Drays will stand behind the girl's word in the justice's court," he says, and he doesn't quite meet your eyes. "I'd have the rest of the truth about my house, too. Later." Isaude takes your hand briefly, and says nothing, and doesn't need to.

You've earned 75 XP for the hearing, and you are at 300, enough for level 2. When you have a moment to rest properly, we'll walk through your choices together.

The arbiter points at the cellar door. "Your quarter hour, mistress. A guard stays at the door, within hearing of a raised voice, not of a low one. He has asked for you again, by name."

Down the stair it is cool and smells of salt-barrels and lamp oil. Corvin sits on an upturned cask in a small stone room with a single lamp, gloves folded on his knee. He looks up as you come in.

"Close the door, Wren," he says gently. "You have fifteen minutes, and I've twenty years of things to say. Ask me the one that matters first."

entries.text:
You don't perform. You say it the way Kit told you to, straight, and the hall listens. Your Persuasion check was a 14. The rehearsal advantage and the exhaustion disadvantage cancel, so it was a single roll, and it clears the bar.

You name the three houses in order and say what each cost. Lord Edric confessed. Lady Maren's village learned the truth. Here, a contract is stayed before it was sealed. When you reach the two weeks you kept the ledger, your voice catches once, and you let it. "I wanted to know if he'd harmed them, or only flattered them. He harmed them." Somewhere behind you a bench creaks. Sir Corwen doesn't look away from you.

The arbiter questions you for half an hour, dry and exact. How did you come by the ledger? Who else has read it? Why a girl who sold tales for nineteen years should be believed now? You answer each, and where you don't know, you say so. Kit is called once to confirm the ride and the road, and says "Aye" three times, which seems to count for a good deal.

At last the arbiter sets down her stylus. "I have heard a forger's apprentice confess more than she needed to," she says. "That is rarer than honesty and more useful. Your sworn account is entered. The Dray leaf is held by this hall, and a copy will go to the keep's justice, and the contract is unsealed until it is read against the rolls. Master Tallowmere will be held for Dame Crowe's assize at Marrowford, and you will be summoned to it." She pauses. "You are free to go, Wren Ashgrove. You will not leave Saltmarsh before the morning."

Sir Corwen rises as the hall begins to empty. He says only, gruffly, "The keep's door is open to you," and goes. Isaude touches your sleeve as she passes and doesn't speak.

It is twenty to three. The guard at the cellar door looks at the arbiter, who gives a short nod toward you. The quarter hour she promised is yours now, with the guard at the door and Kit beside you if you want her there.

You are still hollow with exhaustion and have no spell slots. The Wick-House stands somewhere on the quay, and a staff your mother left is waiting there.

You climb back to the Salt Gull, peel off your wet boots and sleep beside the fire until the light in the shutters has gone from grey to copper. Kit's snore carries on across the room like a slow saw. The storm has blown itself thin. It's a quarter to seven when Pell knocks, hands you a folded sheet, and goes back down to the common room without a word.

Corvin's map is neat and unhurried, in the same black ink he used for all his best forgeries. It shows the lower Marrow below Saltmarsh's road-fork, with a reed-choked bend marked in a small drawn lantern. Beneath it he has written: *Sallow Reach Shrine. Tamsin Orle, keeper. A day and a half upriver from Saltmarsh by the east bank track. You were four, perhaps five. She had a cat called Biscuit. I never lied to you about the cat.* At the bottom, no signature, only the crooked flame.

You check it against what you have. Elowen's letter and the strip of paper name no shrine-house on the lower Marrow, and Brann only repeated her saying that her daughter was "safe among people who will love her." A woman who took coin to keep a child fits that badly, or fits it exactly if Elowen had no choice. The map doesn't contradict anything, which proves nothing from a man who writes true things in order to be believed.

You have no spell slots, one Bardic Inspiration, and a long rest due to finish in the small hours. The arbiter's rider won't be back from Thornhallow for two days or so. What does Wren do?

You sleep the afternoon away by the fire, boots steaming on the hearth, with Kit snoring across the room. The storm wears itself out against the shutters. This is a long nap, not a rest that counts. Your slots are still empty and the exhaustion is still there, because the long rest can't finish before about four tomorrow morning. You wake a little after five. It's dusk, and Bess Harl is banging a ladle on the stair for supper.

Pell comes up as the lamps are lit, rain-dark and awkward in the doorway. He hands you a folded sheet and says, "Straight from his hand to yours, and I didn't read it." He then takes a bowl of stew from Bess and goes to eat it on the landing, where he can hear anyone climbing.

Corvin has drawn the map in his careful, ink-black hand, and it is a good map. A river line runs up from Saltmarsh. About a day and a half upstream, on the east bank, he has drawn a small lantern-shape and named it: the Rushlight Shrine at Withy Reach. Below it he wrote: *The keeper was a goodwife, Annet Sedge. She took Elowen's coin to keep you and ask nothing. I paid her double and took you, in the year you were four or five. If she lives, she'll know your face. If she doesn't, ask who tends the lamp. C.T.* In the corner is the small crooked-flame lantern he used to sign his notes.

You set it beside Elowen's letter and the strip from the lamp-staff. Neither names the Rushlight Shrine or any goodwife, so nothing in your mother's hand confirms it. Nothing contradicts it either. The strip speaks only of the Gullspit light, and the letter says only that you were left "among people who will love her", which could be anyone at all. The map is either true or the best forgery Corvin ever made.

Kit sits up, rubs her face and reads it over your shoulder without comment. Then she says, "Aldous wants the staff, and he's got a ship. He'll know we've got it and where. Staying here, he finds us. Going upriver, we'd be on the road toward Marrowford anyway, for Dame Crowe." She spoons stew. "Withy Reach is on the way. Your call."

So the choices on the table are these. The Rushlight Shrine lies upriver, on the way to Marrowford. The reliquary stays with Brann on the spit, and the arbiter's rider hasn't returned. The Heron's Tithe is still out there. It's about six in the evening, with a hot supper in front of you. What does Wren do?

entries.text:
You sleep the afternoon away beside the fire, with Kit snoring across the room and the storm slowly wearing itself out against the shutters. It isn't a long rest, and your spells stay empty. But you wake with your head clearer, and the light is going amber at the edges. It is about half past six.

Pell comes up the stair at dusk, damp to the knees. He hands you a folded sheet and says nothing, and goes to stand at the landing with his back to the door.

The map is in Corvin's own hand, neat and unhurried, in the ink he uses for pedigrees. A thin river line runs down to the estuary. A day's ride upriver of Saltmarsh, at a bend where reeds crowd the bank, he has drawn a small lantern and labelled it *Sedge Stop, a wayside shrine-house, ferry landing*. Below it: *Dilly Marsh, called Goodwife Sedge. She kept you the winter you were four, and some of the next. Fifteen years gone, or a little more.* At the bottom, a single line: *Everything else I said was craft. This is not.* He has signed it with the little drawn lantern.

You lay it beside Elowen's letter and the strip from the staff and go over them by the lamp. Your Investigation check is a 5 (disadvantage again), and it gets you nothing. Neither paper names a shrine-house or a woman, and your tired eyes find nothing that confirms or contradicts the map. Corvin's hand looks honest, but then it always did. Mother Ysolde Vane has kept the Wick-House thirty years, though. If a Sedge Stop is on the Lantern-Bearer's old roll of wayside shrines, she'd know.

Kit sits up, rubs her face, and pulls the stew pot toward her. Supper is on the table, with bread, fish and a jug of small beer. Bess Harl hovers in the doorway, pretending she isn't listening. Your reliquary still burns in the Gullspit lamp. The arbiter's rider won't be back from Thornhallow for two or three days. Dame Crowe's assize is at the month's end, and your long rest can't finish until about four tomorrow morning. Kit looks at you across the bowl, waiting.

What does Wren decide?

sheet.opening: Wren Ashgrove, a half-elf bard of about nineteen with a quick grin and a sharper tongue, arrives at dusk in the river-market town of Marrowford, a few weeks after fleeing the caravan of her mentor Corvin Tallowmere. She was raised by him as a storyteller's apprentice, and she left in the night at a river crossing with his ledger of forged tales sold to nobles (its pages now hidden in the binding of her road-psalter), a few of his best forgeries, and a head start. She carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, a gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers whom Corvin worshipped only as cover; it holds a curl of yellowed parchment in an unknown hand that may be a true blessing or another forgery. She does not know if Corvin has sent anyone after her. Her ideal: stories should be free, and truth is whatever people can be made to believe. Her bond: find the nobles Corvin cheated and decide whether to expose him or quietly fix what he did. Her flaw: she can't resist a secret, and she lies even when the truth would serve her better. She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. The hook: as she reaches the market square, she spots a caravan wagon with Corvin's painted shrine-lantern sigil parked at the edge of town, but no sign of Corvin. A frightened young page in a minor noble's livery is pressing a sealed letter into the hands of the wagon's driver, and the seal looks like one Wren has seen in the ledger. Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it.
